title: Guru yoga
hookLine: joining one's mind with the teacher's awakened mind

lines: A KID AT A KITCHEN COUNTER.
cards: A kid stands at a kitchen counter beside a grandmother making bread. No recipe card. The kid watches her hands and copies them, badly at first, for years.
Decades later, that kid is kneading dough and notices: these are her hands. Same push, same fold, same little slap at the end. Nobody taught it in words.
It passed across, from one person to another, by being close. Tibetan Buddhism has a practice built on that kind of closeness, the last of the four foundations.

teach.b: First, the words. Guru is Sanskrit for teacher; in Tibetan, lama. Teachers often explain yoga here as joining, so guru yoga is joining with the teacher.
The practitioner visualizes the teacher, usually not as an ordinary person but as an awakened figure from the lineage. In Nyingma practice it's often Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche.
In Gelug practice, a well-known guru yoga centers on Tsongkhapa. The figure appears in the sky ahead, or above the head, bright and kind. Third, receiving.

teach.h: LIGHT TO BODY, SPEECH AND MIND.
teach.b: In versions of the practice, light streams from the teacher's forehead, throat and heart to the practitioner's own: body, speech and mind, the same three the prostrations linked to crown, throat and heart.

The student asks for blessing and receives it as light. Fourth, joining. At the end, the teacher melts into light and dissolves into the practitioner, who rests with no separation between the two minds.
Tibetan teachers explain that what's joined isn't a personality.
It's the awakened mind the teacher stands for, which they say is the student's own nature too.

And one caution from inside the tradition, the one you met in year one: check the teacher. Tibetan texts on the path advise examining a teacher carefully, for a long time, before placing this kind of trust.
Guru yoga rests on a teacher's real goodness. It isn't meant to ask anyone to set their judgment aside.

how: Tibetan Buddhists practice guru yoga as the culmination of the foundational practices and often daily afterward, visualizing the teacher as an awakened figure such as Padmasambhava or Tsongkhapa, receiving blessings and resting with the mind joined to the teacher's.

games.q: you've met a charismatic teacher and want to begin guru yoga with them right away. what do the Tibetan texts on the path advise?
o: trust them at once; doubt is an obstacle.
examine them carefully, for a long time, first.
never trust any teacher at all.
games.why: the texts advise a long, careful look at a teacher's qualities before placing this kind of trust in them.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something good, a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend, a writer you never met, and picture them a little above and in front of you.
Let one quality of theirs come forward: their patience, their honesty, the way they listened.
Breathing in, let that quality come toward you like light; breathing out, let it settle in, until it feels less like theirs and more like yours.

wordCard.voice: Guru yoga. Joining with the teacher: picturing them, receiving their blessing, and resting as one awakened mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit guru: teacher. Tibetan translates it as lama.

carryVoice: Your line: joining minds. Some things pass across only by being close. Day thirteen-oh-eight, done.
